s1-noun~idea.cta: Naming words on the Sentence road
s1-noun~idea.title: Naming words
s1-noun~idea.body: A noun names a person, an animal, a place or a thing: girl, tiger, Delhi, umbrella. If you can put "the" or "a" in front of it, it is often a noun.
s1-noun~idea.more: I can find the nouns in a sentence.

s1-verb~idea.cta: Doing words on the Sentence road
s1-verb~idea.title: Doing words
s1-verb~idea.body: A verb says what someone does or is: run, jumped, is, thought. Ask "what happened?" — the answer is the verb.
s1-verb~idea.more: I can find the verb in a sentence.

s1-verb~story.cta: Doing words on the Sentence road
s1-verb~story.title: Doing words
s1-verb~story.body: Something is always happening in a story. The word that tells you what happens is the verb.

s1-adj~idea.cta: Describing words on the Sentence road
s1-adj~idea.title: Describing words
s1-adj~idea.body: An adjective describes a noun (a RED kite). An adverb describes a verb — how, when or where (she ran QUICKLY).
s1-adj~idea.more: I can find the adjective or adverb in a sentence.

s1-adj~story.cta: Describing words on the Sentence road
s1-adj~story.title: Describing words
s1-adj~story.body: Quill wants every sentence to paint a picture. The words that add colour are adjectives and adverbs.

s1-more~idea.cta: Adverbs, pronouns and prepositions on the Sentence road
s1-more~idea.title: Adverbs, pronouns and prepositions
s1-more~idea.body: An adverb tells you more about a verb: how, when or where something happens (crept QUIETLY). A pronoun stands in for a noun so you do not have to repeat it (Quill → it, Bee and Quill → they). A preposition sits in front of a noun and shows where or when it is: under the gate, after lunch, between the trees.
s1-more~idea.more: I can say whether a word is an adverb, a pronoun or a preposition.

s1-more~story.title: Adverbs, pronouns and prepositions
s1-more~story.body: Quill the fox crept quietly under the gate, and then it looked for Bee. "Three little words in that sentence do three different jobs," says Quill. "Can you spot them?"

wr1-copy~idea.cta: Copy it exactly on the Writing road
wr1-copy~idea.title: Copy it exactly
wr1-copy~idea.body: Copying slowly trains your eye: you notice where the commas fall, which words are capitalised, how a long sentence holds together. Every mistake is a thing you have just learned to see.
wr1-copy~idea.more: I can copy a line from a classic exactly, with every capital and comma.

wr1-copy~story.cta: Copy it exactly on the Writing road
wr1-copy~story.title: Copy it exactly
wr1-copy~story.body: Long ago, children learned to write by copying great sentences — and noticed how they were built.
wr1-copy~story.more: Taught at: Writing 1 · Copywork — Copy it exactly.

wr1-copy~eg.cta: Copy it exactly on the Writing road
wr1-copy~eg.title: Copy it exactly: for example
wr1-copy~eg.body: Copy one line. Then check: spelling, capitals, punctuation.

sp1-aloud~idea.cta: Read it aloud on the Stage
sp1-aloud~idea.title: Read it aloud
sp1-aloud~idea.body: Good reading aloud has a steady pace — about 100 to 150 words a minute — and a small pause at every full stop. The app can measure your time, pace and pauses on this device. It cannot hear expression — you and your grown-up judge that.
sp1-aloud~idea.more: I can read a passage aloud at a steady pace, with pauses at the full stops.

sp1-aloud~story.cta: Read it aloud on the Stage
sp1-aloud~story.title: Read it aloud

li1-who-where~idea.cta: Who and where on the Literature road
li1-who-where~idea.title: Who and where
li1-who-where~idea.body: Characters are the people or animals a story is about; the main character is the one the story follows most. The setting is where (and when) it happens. In The Tale of Peter Rabbit, Peter is the main character, and most of the story is set in Mr. McGregor's vegetable garden.
li1-who-where~idea.more: I can name the main character and the setting of a story.

li1-who-where~story.title: Who and where

li1-problem~idea.cta: What goes wrong? on the Literature road
li1-problem~idea.title: What goes wrong?
li1-problem~idea.body: The problem is what goes wrong, or what a character has to deal with. It is what makes us want to read on.
